explain.say: Fill a jar with muddy river water and leave it on the shelf. Sand drops in seconds, but the water stays cloudy for days, because the finest clay bits are so tiny they barely sink. A water works cannot wait days. So it does three things in a row, shown on the board.

explain.say: Here is a water works in 3D. Look at the flocculation tank and the settling tank next to it: tiny flocs grow, then sink as sludge. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

draw.text: Coagulation, flocculation and settling: Stokes' law in a water works

explain.say: Here is the real machine. In the rapid mix tank a flash mixer spins hard for under a minute while alum is dosed in: that is coagulation, cancelling the charges. Then in the flocculator big paddles turn slowly for twenty to thirty minutes, so the bits bump gently and grow into fluffy flocs. Why slowly? What would fast paddles do to a floc?

They would smash it! Now why bigger is better. Stokes' law says a particle sinks at a speed that grows with the square of its size. Look at the curve: a ten micrometre clay grain sinks at only zero point three two metres per hour. Double the size and it sinks four times faster, about one point three metres per hour.

draw.text: v = g(ρp − ρw)d² / 18μ ≈ 0.0032 d² m/h (d in µm)

explain.say: So how big must the settling tank be? Any particle sinking faster than the overflow rate, the flow divided by the tank's surface area, will settle out. Our works sends six hundred and twenty five cubic metres an hour into six hundred and twenty five square metres of tank: one metre per hour. See the cut-off mark: grains bigger than about seventeen point six micrometres are caught.

explain.say: Operators choose the alum dose with a jar test: six jars, six doses, stirred like the plant, and the clearest jar wins. Well done! Exam tip: the overflow rate has units of a speed, so compare it straight with the settling speed. Challenge: a grain three times bigger than ten micrometres, how fast does it sink?

faq.a: Coagulation is the fast mixing of a chemical such as alum into raw water to cancel the negative charges on tiny particles, so they stop repelling each other and can stick together.
Flocculation is the slow, gentle stirring that follows coagulation, for about 20 to 30 minutes, so the destabilised particles bump together and grow into large flocs that settle.
Stokes' law gives the settling speed of a small sphere in a fluid: g times the density difference times the diameter squared, over 18 times the viscosity. Speed grows with the square of size.

faq.q: What is the overflow rate of a settling tank?
faq.a: The overflow rate is the flow divided by the tank surface area. Every particle that settles faster than this speed is removed; 625 cubic metres per hour over 625 square metres gives 1 metre per hour.
asks: How do you size a sedimentation tank?

faq.a: A jar test is a bench test where several jars of raw water get different coagulant doses and are stirred like the plant. The dose giving the clearest water is chosen.
asks: How is the alum dose chosen?

facts: George Gabriel Stokes published his law for the drag on a slow-moving sphere in 1851.
Aluminium sulphate (alum) and ferric chloride are the most common coagulants in water treatment.

quiz.say: A settling tank takes 1,200 cubic metres per hour, and the overflow rate must be 1.5 metres per hour. What surface area does it need?

wrong.1: That multiplies by the overflow rate instead of dividing.

quiz.say: By Stokes' law, doubling a particle's diameter makes it settle…
quiz.show: By Stokes' law, doubling a particle's diameter makes it settle…
quiz.why: Settling speed grows with the diameter squared: 2² = 4.

wrong.1: Speed is not proportional to size, but to size squared.
wrong.2: Size matters a lot; that is why flocculation grows the particles.
